clue.text: Scriptural writing wrongly interpreted as trash

indicators.note: something wrongly interpreted is misread, so these letters are taken in a different order

explanation.surface: A sacred text has been misread as rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hindu sacred treatise on doctrine or law is a piece of scriptural writing.

clue.text: Most of California's capital in solemn pledge

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter is kept here

parts.note: Sacramento is the state capital of California

explanation.surface: Much of the Californian capital is caught up in a solemn vow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' trims the final O from SACRAMENTO; 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In older usage a sacrament is an oath or solemn vow, from the Latin for a soldier's oath of allegiance.

clue.text: Confused Ephesian wife recalled in an air dangerously evocative

indicators.note: recalled is read as called back, so the letters found are taken in the reverse direction
in signals letters sitting inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A muddled wife from Ephesus is remembered in a perilously suggestive song.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside 'an air da(ngerously)' sits ANAIRDA; 'recalled' turns it round. In The Comedy of Errors Adriana, wife of Antipholus of Ephesus, is bewildered by the twins.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors the married woman of Ephesus, baffled by the mix-up of twin husbands, bears this name.

clue.text: They are invited to a staged performance

definitions.text: They are invited to a staged performance

parts.words: They are invited to a staged performance
parts.note: read plainly, people asked to come to a show; read as a title, the name of a play put on stage

explanation.surface: Those with invitations come to watch a play.
explanation.definitionFit: People who receive invitations are visitors, and the phrase is also the title of a stage play.

clue.text: Doré illustrated execution of this king said to be cruel, apparently a joke

definitions.text: Doré illustrated execution of this king said to be cruel

parts.note: a gag is a joke

explanation.surface: An engraver pictured a cruel king's death, which seems a laughing matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Gustave Doré engraved Samuel hewing the Amalekite king in pieces (1 Samuel 15), the king whose sword had 'made women childless'; 'apparently' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amalekite ruler slain by Samuel in 1 Samuel 15 is the monarch whose death Doré engraved.

clue.text: Essayist shows supplement is viable

parts.note: to supplement is to add to
taken as written
a viable plan is on, possible

explanation.surface: A writer of essays demonstrates that an extra is workable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'viable' gives ON as in 'the deal is on', meaning feasible; 'shows' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Addison, co-founder of The Spectator, is a celebrated English essayist.

clue.text: A base paint, perhaps, to rename

definitions.note: a verb phrase for a noun answer: the sect member is one who names (baptises) again

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: the words as printed give A BASE PAINT; the setter's intended fodder, with bast (plant fibre) for base, supplies the second T

explanation.surface: A coat of undercoat might need relabelling.
explanation.walkthrough: As printed the fodder gives an E where the answer needs a second T, so the anagram falls one letter short; the parse treats 'base' as the setter's slip for 'bast'.
explanation.definitionFit: The radical Reformation sect insisted on baptising adults again, and baptism is a christening, a naming.

clue.text: Theatrical byway

parts.note: a London street famous for its playhouse, named with the word that precedes Lane

explanation.surface: A side street associated with the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Drury Lane in London's West End is home to the Theatre Royal, the oldest working theatre site in the city.
explanation.definitionFit: The West End lane holding the Theatre Royal is the capital's most theatrical side street.

clue.text: O'Brian created a mate for him

definitions.text: O'Brian created a mate for him

parts.words: O'Brian created a mate for him
parts.note: Patrick O'Brian wrote Stephen Maturin as Jack Aubrey's ship's doctor and friend; a naval doctor's assistant is also his 'mate'

explanation.surface: The novelist invented a companion for this man.
explanation.walkthrough: Patrick O'Brian's naval novels pair Captain Aubrey with Maturin, the ship's medical officer; on a warship that officer's assistant was the 'surgeon's mate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Maturin serves as the medical man aboard ship, and naval medical officers had assistants called mates.

clue.text: His traveller was out of luck

definitions.text: His traveller was out of luck

parts.words: His traveller was out of luck
parts.note: Thomas ... wrote The Unfortunate Traveller, a picaresque tale of 1594

explanation.surface: This man's wayfarer had no good fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elizabethan pamphleteer wrote The Unfortunate Traveller, whose hero is a luckless wanderer.

clue.text: Chef begins with cooked rice, as one who could work magic

indicators.note: begins points to the opening letter of the word before it
cooked rice is rice worked over, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A chef starts with boiled rice, like a kitchen wizard.
explanation.walkthrough: Chef and kitchen dress up an enchantress: Circe's magic in the Odyssey also worked through food and drink she served Odysseus's crew.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Odyssey the enchantress of Aeaea turns Odysseus's men into swine, a sorceress.

clue.text: Xerxes possibly Hausa, not quite sure in the end

indicators.note: not quite right, so the combined letters are disordered and reassembled

explanation.surface: A Persian king might be a West African people, though one can't be certain in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' shuffles HAUSA and SURE together; 'in the end' is a link. The Book of Esther's king is often identified with Xerxes, hence 'possibly'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian monarch of the Book of Esther is usually identified with the historical Xerxes I.

clue.text: Commander gets public transport for prophet of famine

parts.note: an aga is a Turkish commander or chief officer
a bus is public transport

explanation.surface: An officer catches a bus to see a doom-sayer.
explanation.walkthrough: In Acts 11:28 this prophet foretold a great famine; 'gets' and 'for' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: In Acts the Christian seer from Jerusalem predicts a great dearth over all the world.

clue.text: Shakespeare's cross-dresser who courted Woolf's transsexual?

definitions.text: Shakespeare's cross-dresser who courted Woolf's transsexual?

parts.words: Shakespeare's cross-dresser who courted Woolf's transsexual?
parts.note: in As You Like It Rosalind disguises herself as a youth and is wooed by Orlando, also the name of Virginia Woolf's sex-changing hero

explanation.surface: A literary in-joke: Rosalind in disguise wooing Woolf's gender-shifting hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly Orlando courts the disguised Rosalind; the clue swaps in Woolf's Orlando, who changes sex mid-novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Disguised as a boy in As You Like It, Rosalind takes the alias of Jove's cupbearer.

clue.text: "… kill this lecherous itch with drinking water, /Or live, like a -, on poor-john" (Massinger, The Guardian)

definitions.text: "… kill this lecherous itch with drinking water, /Or live, like a -, on poor-john" (Massinger, The Guardian)

parts.words: "… kill this lecherous itch with drinking water, /Or live, like a -, on poor-john" (Massinger, The Guardian)
parts.note: a gap in Massinger's lines asks for a monk famed for water and salted fish, poor-john being dried hake

explanation.surface: A line of Massinger with a word missing: subdue lust by abstinence.
explanation.walkthrough: The Carthusians are a strict contemplative order living on plain fare; poor-john is cheap dried salt fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Monks of the order founded by St Bruno at La Chartreuse keep perpetual abstinence from meat.

clue.text: Scott's PO

parts.note: Petty Officer Edgar of that surname died on Captain Scott's return from the South Pole

explanation.surface: The petty officer on Scott's expedition.
explanation.definitionFit: Petty Officer Edgar, a Welshman, was one of the polar party that died with Scott in 1912.

clue.text: "This is the chase", he said, "I am gone for ever" (his pursuer not mentioned in the cast)

definitions.text: "This is the chase", he said, "I am gone for ever" (his pursuer not mentioned in the cast)

parts.words: "This is the chase", he said, "I am gone for ever" (his pursuer not mentioned in the cast)
parts.note: the courtier in The Winter's Tale who speaks these words just before the direction 'Exit, pursued by a bear'; the bear has no place in the list of characters

explanation.surface: A character's last words before the famous stage chase.
explanation.walkthrough: The Winter's Tale (III.iii): he leaves the infant Perdita and exits pursued by a bear, which is not listed in the dramatis personae. The grid's spelling ends -ES.
explanation.definitionFit: Paulina's husband in The Winter's Tale speaks these lines just before the bear chases him offstage.

clue.text: He felt he could speak English as well as Percy

definitions.text: He felt he could speak English as well as Percy

parts.words: He felt he could speak English as well as Percy
parts.note: in Henry IV Part 1 the Welsh chieftain tells Hotspur 'I can speak English, lord, as well as you'

explanation.surface: A man confident his English matched Percy's.
explanation.walkthrough: Hotspur is Harry Percy; the Welsh rebel answers his mockery with 'I can speak English, lord, as well as you' (III.i).
explanation.definitionFit: Owen, the Welsh rebel of Henry IV Part 1, boasts to Hotspur that his English is as good as the Englishman's.

clue.text: Heavyweight poet, displacing seven tons

indicators.note: displacing moves letters out of place, so the phrase is rearranged

explanation.surface: A hefty versifier shifting a load of seven tons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'displacing' rearranges SEVEN TONS. The name covers both Teófilo, the Cuban Olympic heavyweight boxer, and Robert Louis, author of A Child's Garden of Verses.
explanation.definitionFit: Teófilo of that surname was a triple Olympic heavyweight boxing champion, and Robert Louis wrote verse.

clue.text: Slanderous slave sits there, stirring it up

indicators.note: stirring things up mixes them, so the words are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: A mischievous servant lounges about, causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirring it up' rearranges SITS THERE. In Troilus and Cressida he is the scurrilous railer in the Greek camp.
explanation.definitionFit: The foul-mouthed Greek of Troilus and Cressida is a deformed railer whom Ajax calls a slave.

clue.text: Fatally drunken Greek, addressed by Pound as "our Friend"

definitions.text: Fatally drunken Greek, addressed by Pound as "our Friend"

parts.words: Fatally drunken Greek, addressed by Pound as "our Friend"
parts.note: the youngest of Odysseus's crew, who fell drunk from Circe's roof and is greeted in Pound's Canto I

explanation.surface: A drunk Greek who died, hailed as a friend by the poet.
explanation.walkthrough: In Odyssey X–XI the sailor falls from Circe's roof after drinking and breaks his neck; Pound's first Canto meets his shade.
explanation.definitionFit: Odysseus's crewman died falling drunk from Circe's roof and is hailed as 'our friend' in Canto I.

clue.text: "Thou art not so much as Bastard" (Wycherley, The Plain Dealer)

definitions.text: "Thou art not so much as Bastard" (Wycherley, The Plain Dealer)

parts.words: "Thou art not so much as Bastard" (Wycherley, The Plain Dealer)
parts.note: the missing word is an old legal term meaning eldest, so the line jeers that he is not even the eldest illegitimate son

explanation.surface: A Restoration insult with its final word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In old law 'bastard eigne' was the elder illegitimate son of parents who later married; the quotation drops that last word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norman French law term means first-born or eldest, as in 'bastard eigne'.

clue.text: He observed the effects of air movement in the salices

definitions.text: He observed the effects of air movement in the salices

parts.words: He observed the effects of air movement in the salices
parts.note: salices is Latin for willows, and air movement is wind: a disguised title of a 1908 children's novel

explanation.surface: A naturalist watched breezes stirring the willows.
explanation.walkthrough: Salix is the willow genus, plural salices, so 'air movement in the salices' is The Wind in the Willows, by Kenneth of that surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth, the Scottish author, wrote The Wind in the Willows, about river-bank creatures.

clue.text: Seventh forename featured by Hawthorne

parts.note: a Latin given name meaning seventh, also the title hero of Hawthorne's unfinished romance Septimius Felton

explanation.surface: A name meaning seventh that appears in Hawthorne.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin forename traditionally given to a seventh child appears in Hawthorne's posthumous romance.

clue.text: Whose, in fact, was "Chesterton's nightmare"?

parts.note: Chesterton subtitled The Man Who Was Thursday 'A Nightmare'; its poet-detective hero is Gabriel of this surname, so the answer is his name with a possessive

explanation.surface: A question about who owned Chesterton's bad dream.
explanation.walkthrough: The Man Who Was Thursday: A Nightmare follows Gabriel, the poet turned policeman; read as a possessive his surname answers 'Whose?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The bad dream of Chesterton's subtitle is lived through by Gabriel, the novel's hero, so it is his.

clue.text: Provenance of Murdoch's girl

parts.note: Iris Murdoch wrote The Italian Girl (1964), so her girl comes from that country

explanation.surface: Where the novelist's young woman came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris Murdoch's novel The Italian Girl names its heroine by her Mediterranean homeland.

clue.text: Imagine an excerpt from Enderby Outside, a tender scene

indicators.note: an excerpt is a short passage taken out of a longer text, so the letters lie within the words

explanation.surface: Picture a gentle passage from Burgess's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'outsIDE A TEnder'. Enderby Outside is an Anthony Burgess novel, a decoy for the run.
explanation.definitionFit: To form an idea in the mind is to conceive or picture it.

clue.text: Little sparrow with no regrets

explanation.surface: A small bird that is sorry for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Édith Piaf's stage name is Parisian slang for sparrow, and her signature song was 'Non, je ne regrette rien'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French chanteuse's nickname meant 'little sparrow', and she sang that she regretted nothing.

clue.text: Latin main character from Nicholas Nickleby could produce

indicators.note: the two words could produce a new name when their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Dickens's figure might be made from Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could produce' rearranges LATIN MAIN. Mr Mantalini is the dandy husband of Madame Mantalini the dressmaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, the foppish spendthrift husband of the milliner in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby, bears this name.

clue.text: Burns kids

parts.note: read as the Scots poet's word for children, not as a verb with kids burning

explanation.surface: A grim sentence about scorching children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burns' is Robert Burns; the Scots word for little ones, 'wee ane', appears in his verse.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, the dialect of Robert Burns, small children are called by this word.

clue.text: A native American writer

parts.note: suggests an indigenous author but means simply an American-born writer, of Armenian descent

explanation.surface: An Indigenous author from the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native American' suggests an Indigenous author, but William of this surname was a Californian-born writer of Armenian parentage (The Human Comedy).
explanation.definitionFit: William, author of The Human Comedy, was born in Fresno, California, so a United States novelist by birth.

clue.text: Prolific novelist a long way in advance including first French person

indicators.note: including means one piece takes the other inside it

parts.note: far means a long way
on means ahead, in advance, as in 'further on'
je is French for I, the first person singular

explanation.surface: A productive writer leads by a distance, taking in the first Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'person' here is the grammatical person: French 'je' is the first-person pronoun. 'Including' puts it inside the run for a long way in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: J. Jefferson of that surname wrote some sixty thrillers, and his sister Eleanor was equally productive.
